eoce-078.title: Lake Wanapitei impact
eoce-078.text: A lake inside a city fills an old crater. An impact about 37.2 million years ago made an 8.4 km crater, now Lake Wanapitei, within the city of Greater Sudbury, Ontario, Canada. It lies next to the nearby but unrelated Sudbury impact crater. It is one of the world's largest lakes entirely within a single municipality.

eoce-079.title: The Cascade volcanoes awaken
eoce-079.text: Volcanism in the Cascade arc of the Pacific Northwest began about 37 million years ago. The West Cascades period, 37 to 17 million years ago, was a time of exceptionally active volcanoes. The arc now includes nearly 20 major volcanoes among over 4,000 separate volcanic vents. In the North Cascades geologists have not identified with certainty any volcanic rocks as old as 35 million years.

eoce-083.title: The Mistastin impact in Labrador
eoce-083.text: A crater in Labrador was spotted from space. An impact about 36.6 million years ago left a crater originally about 28 km across, in northwestern inland Labrador, due west of Natuashish, near Quebec. Mistastin Lake was first identified as a possible impact crater in 1968, after being viewed from space. Cubic zirconia around the rim suggests temperatures above 2,370 °C, roughly 43% of the temperature of the Sun's surface.

eoce-089.title: The Ring of Fire takes its modern shape
eoce-089.text: By about 35 million years ago the Kula and Farallon plates had been subducted, and the Pacific plate was ringed by subduction much like today's Ring of Fire. The New Zealand subduction zone, the last of its present segments, formed about 35 million years ago. The ring is not complete: it does not extend across the southern Pacific from New Zealand to the Antarctic Peninsula or the southern tip of South America, because plate boundaries there are divergent. The southwest is more complex, with smaller plates colliding with the Pacific plate at the Mariana Islands, the Philippines, eastern Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and New Zealand.

eoce-092.title: Florissant, a lake of fossils
eoce-092.text: Falling algae buried a forest's leftovers. In Colorado, diatom blooms in a lake dammed by volcanic mudflows finely preserved late Eocene plants and insects. As diatoms fell to the lake bottom, plants and animals that had recently died were preserved by the diatom falls. The site is also known for petrified stumps of giant sequoia relatives. Fossil plants, especially leaves, have been the most useful source of information on paleoclimate during deposition of the Florissant Formation.

olig-004.title: Baikal's rift starts pulling apart again
olig-004.text: Rifting in the Baikal Rift Zone resumed in the Oligocene, later forming graben basins, which are down-dropped blocks of crust. Lake Baikal in Siberia is a modern example of a rift basin.

olig-005.title: Carnivorans seize the top predator roles
olig-005.text: Cats and their kin took over the hunt. Carnivorans, led by the cat-like nimravids, took the top-predator roles held in the Eocene by oxyaenids and mesonychians. Dogs, nimravids, bears, weasels and raccoons began to replace the creodonts in the Old World. The teeth hint that the groups were separate: carnassial teeth sit near the front of the molar row in carnivorans but near the back in creodonts, suggesting separate evolutionary histories and an order-level distinction.

olig-013.title: The Obik Sea drains and Europe meets Asia
olig-013.text: A sea disappeared and animals walked across its bed. The Obik Sea, which had separated Europe from Asia, retreated early in the Oligocene and left a lasting land connection. Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait across it, opening Europe to Asian mammals. Sea levels were lower in the Oligocene than in the early Eocene, exposing large coastal plains in Europe. By the end of the Eocene-Oligocene transition they had dropped by 105 meters. That transition in Europe and Asia has been called the Grande Coupure.

olig-022.title: The Atacama begins its long drought
olig-022.text: Earth's oldest desert may be in Chile. A proto-Humboldt Current, set up with the Tasmania–Antarctic passage about 33 million years ago, began the Atacama's drying. Humid air was generally lacking there afterward, apart from brief wetter spells. Aridity predates the rise of the Central Andes, but hyper-aridity is generally thought to have resulted from that rise. The driest part lies between the Andes and the Chilean Coast Range, which block moisture from both the Pacific and the Atlantic in a two-sided rain shadow.

olig-028.title: An asteroid strikes Arctic Devon Island
olig-028.text: An impactor about 2 km wide struck Devon Island in Arctic Canada, leaving a crater about 23 km across that exposes rock from as deep as 1,700 m. Its age has been revised several times. The crater's own page gives 31–32 million years, in the Oligocene. But later analyses cited by the Oligocene page put it at 39 Ma, in the Eocene, and call the Oligocene date questionable. The date remains contested.

olig-053.title: Embrithopods leave the record
olig-053.text: Embrithopods, an order of Afro-Arabian mammals, arose in the Early Eocene and were last recorded in the latest Oligocene. Why they vanished is debated. Some experts think they could not compete with invading mammals because of their generalized habits and phyletic conservatism, a tendency to stay unchanged.

olig-056.title: The first elephantimorphs
olig-056.text: Elephantimorphs, the proboscidean group that includes mastodons and modern elephants, first appeared in the Late Oligocene. One timeline dates the first true elephants to about 26 million years ago. These animals reshaped their surroundings: like modern elephants, gomphotheres may have knocked down trees, creating open landscapes.

olig-058.title: Notoungulates grow teeth that never stop
olig-058.text: Teeth that never stop growing helped a South American group diversify. Several notoungulate families separately evolved high-crowned, ever-growing cheek teeth, and such species made up most notoungulates from the Late Oligocene. Notoungulates make up over half the described diversity of South America's native ungulates, with over 150 genera in 14 families. They were morphologically diverse, with forms resembling animals as different as rabbits and rhinoceroses. They and other native ungulates reached their apex of diversity during the Eocene and Oligocene.

olig-060.title: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first forms
olig-060.text: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first formed about 27 million years ago, probably fed partly by glaciers from the older East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It is a marine ice sheet: most of its ice rests on rock and sediment well below sea level, which would be ocean floor without the ice. Because the whole sheet is grounded below sea level, it is vulnerable to geologically rapid ice loss. It declined somewhat during the warm early Pliocene, about five to three million years ago, and the Ross Sea opened up.

olig-065.title: Central America begins to close its seaway
olig-065.text: By the Oligocene, the Central American volcanic arc began colliding with northwestern South America. The collision that closed the Central American Seaway started about 25 million years ago. The setting had been prepared earlier: during the Eocene, about 45 Ma, subduction of the Farallon plate along the Central American subduction zone was re-established.

olig-069.title: The Sea of Japan begins to open
olig-069.text: Around 25 million years ago the Sea of Japan began to open, separating Japan from the mainland and forming today's island arc. It is a modern example of back-arc spreading, a modest ocean basin opened between the volcanic arc of Japan and the Asian mainland.

olig-074.title: Seals arrive and nautiloids vanish
olig-074.text: The earliest pinnipeds, the seal group, appeared about 24 million years ago, near the end of the Oligocene. They belong to the suborder Caniformia of the order Carnivora. Their closest living relatives are musteloids (weasels, raccoons, skunks and red pandas), from which they diverged about 50 million years ago. Their arrival had a cost for others: from the Oligocene on, nautiloids vanished from each region as pinnipeds appeared there.

olig-076.title: Creodonts retreat to Africa
olig-076.text: At the end of the Oligocene, creodonts died out everywhere except Africa and the Middle East. Africa was relatively isolated and kept its endemic fauna.

mioc-001.title: Africa's plants lose ground to the seasons
mioc-001.text: Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start of the Miocene, probably because seasons became more pronounced. Through the epoch the climate slowly cooled towards a series of ice ages. Africa's equatorial forest belt broke apart and rejoined repeatedly during that time.

mioc-007.title: The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape
mioc-007.text: Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene. Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns, which were linked to northern glacial periods. Meanwhile, topographic changes in Africa weakened the Somali Jet while South Asian Summer Monsoon rainfall increased.

mioc-009.title: Diatoms move into fresh water
mioc-009.text: Marine diatoms radiated in the Cretaceous, but freshwater diatoms did not appear until the Miocene. Miocene diatom diversity rose as carbon dioxide and global temperatures fell. Most modern lineages of diatoms had appeared by the Late Miocene.

mioc-011.title: Kelp forests rise in Miocene seas
mioc-011.text: Underwater forests are a Miocene invention. Kelp forests first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems. With grasslands, they were one of two new biomes that supported much of Miocene life. Kelp forests are formed by brown macroalgae and provide a unique habitat for marine organisms. A wide range of sea life, including fish, uses them for protection or food. Especially productive ones tend to occur where oceanographic upwelling delivers cool, nutrient-rich water from depth to the surface layer.

mioc-012.title: Necrolestes, last of an ancient line
mioc-012.text: Meridiolestidans dominated Late Cretaceous South America, and the last of them lived in the Miocene of Patagonia. That last was the mole-like burrowing insectivore Necrolestes, 50 million years after the previous known member. They are generally classified within Cladotheria, closer to living marsupials and placental mammals than to monotremes, though one study recovered them as sister to spalacotheriid 'symmetrodonts'. A possible meridiolestidan is known from a tooth fragment, now lost, from the Eocene La Meseta Formation of the Antarctic Peninsula.

mioc-015.title: Sloth families multiply
mioc-015.text: Sloths diversified in the Miocene, when the major sloth families appeared; diversity waxed and waned, then declined at the epoch's end. A basal sloth group had already colonized the Antilles by the early Miocene. Ground sloths evolved early, in the late Paleogene and Neogene, while South America was isolated. They ranged from under 100 kilograms in the Caribbean forms to 3,700–4,100 kilograms in the largest genera Megatherium, Lestodon and Eremotherium.

mioc-016.title: Snakes boom in North America
mioc-016.text: Snakes were once a minor part of North American fauna, then rose sharply in number and diversity during the Miocene. Vipers and elapids first appeared in North America, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera. The expansion of grasslands there led to an explosive radiation among snakes.

mioc-017.title: South America's native hoofed mammals thin out
mioc-017.text: South America's native hoofed mammals were losing ground. Notoungulates lost 45% of their families in the Miocene, though species numbers stayed stable. By the late Miocene, litopterns and notoungulates were the only surviving native ungulate groups. They had peaked in diversity in the Eocene and Oligocene. Their diversity declined further during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, at the same time as the Great American Interchange let North American ungulates and other mammals enter South America.

mioc-020.title: The Alboran Basin and the Betic Corridor open
mioc-020.text: Between 23 and 20 million years ago, spreading thinned the crust south of Spain to 12-15 km, forming the Alboran Basin. Rotation of Iberia in the early Miocene opened the Betic Corridor, a strait joining the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. The Valencia Trough opened between the Late Oligocene and early Miocene, at the same time as the Provençal Basin.

mioc-023.title: East Antarctic glaciers come and go
mioc-023.text: Antarctic ice was not a steady sheet. East Antarctica probably held some glaciers during the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago, and the Ross Sea margin of its ice sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene. Global temperatures stayed fairly steady through the Oligocene and early Miocene, and Antarctic glaciation waned. About 15 million years ago the Southern Hemisphere ice cap began to grow to its present form, as oceans cooled partly from the Antarctic Circumpolar Current.

mioc-029.title: New Zealand almost drowns
mioc-029.text: About 22 million years ago only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level. This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa. The land is part of Zealandia, a submerged mass that includes present-day New Zealand and would be considered a continent.

mioc-030.title: Tibet sinks, then rises again
mioc-030.text: Tibet sank before it climbed. After sinking about 900 m between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago, the Tibetan Plateau rose by 500 to 1,000 m, between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago. It is the world's largest and highest plateau above sea level, with an area of 2,500,000 square kilometres. The Indo-Australian plate is still driven under it, pushing it up at about 5 mm per year, though erosion reduces the actual gain in height.

mioc-033.title: Conifers and cycads branch out
mioc-033.text: About 20 million years ago some conifer and cycad groups began to diversify as conditions changed. These are gymnosperms, a group that also includes seed ferns and ginkgos and that could reproduce by seeds from the Devonian.

mioc-034.title: Rising rift shoulders split Africa's great rivers
mioc-034.text: Around 20 million years ago the western flank of the East African Rift rose, cutting the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin. Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and Ethiopian and Ugandan rivers did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile. Today the region holds the source of the Nile and several large lakes of its system, including Lake Victoria, Lake Albert, Lake George and Lake Edward. The rift is an intracontinental rift basin with active volcanism.

mioc-055.title: Steens Mountain catches the magnetic field flipping
mioc-055.text: Lava flows caught the field in the act of flipping. At Steens Mountain, Oregon, they recorded a reversal about 16.7 Ma, suggesting the field can shift up to 6 degrees a day. The reversal ending Chron C5Cr contained a series of reversals and excursions. At Battle Mountain, Nevada, lava flows show a brief, several-year-long interval in a reversal when the field direction changed by over 50 degrees. During a reversal the field does not vanish completely, and many poles may form chaotically in different places until it stabilizes again.

mioc-062.title: Australia begins to collide with Southeast Asia
mioc-062.text: In the Middle Miocene, Australia began to collide with Southeast Asia. The collision blocked equatorial ocean flow between the western Pacific and Indian Oceans. Australia had been alone for a long time: by 50 Ma it had separated from Antarctica.

mioc-064.title: Most modern seed plants appear
mioc-064.text: Many new plants evolved in the mid-Miocene, including 95% of modern seed plants. Seed reproduction developed in the Devonian among gymnosperms, but flowering plants evolved millions of years later, in the Cretaceous.

mioc-067.title: Earth's magnetic field flips again and again
mioc-067.text: At least 51 geomagnetic reversals occurred in a 12-million-year period centred on 15 million years ago. In a period of 3 million years centred on 24 Ma, 13 reversals occurred. Overall there have been at least 183 reversals over the last 83 million years, on average one about every 450,000 years. Eras of frequent reversals have been balanced by a few superchrons, long periods with no reversals.

mioc-076.title: The Chile Triple Junction forms
mioc-076.text: The Antarctic Plate began subducting beneath South America about 14 million years ago, forming the Chile Triple Junction, and the Chile Ridge collided with South America near Tierra del Fuego. The asthenospheric window linked to the junction disturbed mantle convection beneath Patagonia, causing an uplift of about 1 km that reversed the Oligocene–Miocene transgression. As the southern Nazca Plate and Chile Rise were consumed by subduction, the junction advanced north. It now lies offshore the Taitao Peninsula at 46°15' S.

mioc-079.title: The Sea of Japan opens at both ends
mioc-079.text: By 14 million years ago the Sea of Japan back-arc basin was open to the northeast and southwest, and rising seas further isolated Japan. The sea is a modest ocean basin that opened by back-arc spreading between the volcanic arc of the Japanese islands and the Asian mainland.
